questions.model: Mara finds it among the reeds; it is by the river / down the bank.
lookFor: Two accurate distinct details about the location, for example reeds and riverbank.
questions.acceptable: Any two independent precise details from the opening that answer where the bell is found.

questions.model: Mara seems protective or uneasy because she pulls the bell away before she can explain why. Her voice sounds more certain than she feels, suggesting she is unsure about the bell but already believes it matters.
lookFor: Clear inference about protectiveness, concern or uncertainty.
Specific evidence, particularly Mara pulling the bell away or sounding more certain than she feels.
Explanation linking the evidence to her emotions.
questions.acceptable: Well-supported alternative interpretations, such as fear of damage or a sense of responsibility.
questions.guidance: Award up to 4 for inference with accurate quotation and explanation; avoid treating one exact phrase as the only correct evidence.

questions.model: The river is unusually calm: its surface holds the sky “without a single wrinkle”. The image suggests stillness, which feels mysterious because the river usually “argued with the stones”. The contrast makes the discovery seem significant.
lookFor: Suitable word or phrase from the river description.
Accurate explanation of a language choice.
Effect on atmosphere supported by the text.
questions.acceptable: Analysis of “argued with the stones” as personification or of “held the sky” as calm reflective imagery.
questions.guidance: Credit analysis rather than simply naming a technique.

questions.model: At first Mara is curious and observant when she brushes the weed off the bell. She becomes protective when Eli reaches for it, then increasingly thoughtful, recognising her grandmother’s stars. By the end she sees it as a “question” to answer rather than a lost object.
lookFor: Beginning and ending moments are compared.
Evidence from two different points.
Explanation of how her outlook changes.
questions.acceptable: Other coherent readings supported by relevant moments.
questions.guidance: Credit development over time, not a plot retelling alone.

questions.model: Mara initially appears curious because she notices the old bell among the reeds and looks closely at its details. The river’s stillness makes the discovery seem unusual: the surface holds the sky “without a single wrinkle”. When Eli tries to touch the bell, she pulls it away before she knows why; this action hints at uncertainty as well as a wish to protect it. The three stars connect the object to family memories and deepen her interest. In the final paragraph, the bell feels like a “question” left for her to answer. This metaphor shows that curiosity has become a responsibility to uncover the past. Through Mara’s changing behaviour and the recurring mystery of the river, the writer presents a character who wants answers but is not yet confident about what those answers may mean.
lookFor: Interpretation and coherent argument (up to 5)
Relevant and integrated textual evidence (up to 5)
Explanation of language or structural choices and effects (up to 5)
Organisation and development across paragraphs (up to 3)
Control of expression, punctuation and grammar (up to 2)
questions.acceptable: Interpretations may vary; award marks according to qualities and evidence, not by matching model wording.
questions.guidance: Human marking required. Five criteria with caps 5,5,5,3,2. Parent can allocate an integer to each.

questions.model: On Monday, Mara and Eli were walking by the river. They had gone there early because the weather was clear. Mara put the bell carefully in her bag.
lookFor: monday → Monday
was walking → were walking
had went → had gone
weather were → weather was
careful → carefully
questions.acceptable: Other wording which preserves the meaning and corrects all five errors.
questions.guidance: Award one mark for each of the five corrected errors.
